messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night of the factory fire, Javier had been the last person to leave his shift. He was a QA engineer at a small chemical plant on the outskirts of Houston, and his job was to verify the pressure readings on a storage tank before the night crew took over. He remembered the gauge needle trembling at the red line, remembered logging the reading into the system, remembered the supervisor telling him it was fine, just a calibration glitch, go home. He went home. Two hours later, the tank ruptured. The explosion killed three night-shift workers—men Javier had waved to on his way out, men whose names he knew. He had checked the tank, and he had left, and they had died.

In the months that followed, Javier’s mind became a loop of that single decision: what if he had refused to sign off, what if he had stayed to argue, what if he had called someone higher up. He found himself replaying the evening in exhaustive detail, not because he wanted to, but because his thoughts seemed to have no other destination. He would be sitting at his desk at his new job—a smaller tech firm where no one knew about the fire—and suddenly he would be back in the plant, watching the gauge, feeling the weight of the clipboard in his hands. The counterfactuals were relentless. He had come to believe that he should have protected those men, that his failure to do so was not a mistake but a moral fact. He was certain that if he had acted differently, they would still be alive. No amount of logic from friends or coworkers could dislodge this conviction; it felt like the only truth he had left.

The world began to feel dangerous in a way it never had before. Javier started noticing things he used to ignore: the way a stranger’s eyes lingered on him in the grocery store, the way a car idling too long at a stoplight seemed like a threat. He had never thought of himself as a fearful person, but now he was certain that anyone could be a source of harm. You can never know who will hurt you, he told himself. The police presence in his neighborhood, once just background noise, now made his chest tighten. He avoided eye contact with officers, crossed the street to avoid passing near a patrol car. He knew this was irrational—the police had nothing to do with the fire—but his body reacted before his mind could catch up.

Television became impossible. News reports about industrial accidents, even brief mentions of fires or explosions, sent him into a dissociative fog. He would feel his surroundings grow distant, his own hands unfamiliar, as if he were watching himself from across a room. He stopped watching the evening news. He stopped scrolling through headlines on his phone. He told his roommate he was just trying to cut down on screen time, but the truth was that any story about a disaster felt like a mirror he could not bear to look into. Even casual talk among coworkers about car crashes or workplace injuries made him excuse himself to the bathroom, where he would stand gripping the sink until the feeling of unreality passed.

His life narrowed. He stopped going out with friends because someone might bring up current events. He stopped driving past the old plant, taking a longer route to work that added twenty minutes to his commute. At work, he found himself unable to concentrate on code reviews, his mind drifting to the thought that nothing good could happen to him anymore. He had begun to believe that his future had been cancelled the night of the fire, that whatever came next would be hollow. He was twenty-four years old, and he felt ancient.

What finally brought Javier to therapy was a panic attack during a team meeting. A colleague mentioned a news article about a factory explosion in another state, and Javier felt the room dissolve. He could not speak, could not move, could not remember where he was. His manager pulled him aside afterward and asked if he was okay. Javier said he was fine, but he knew he was not. He made an appointment the next day. He is not sure what he expects from therapy—he is not even sure he deserves to feel better—but he is tired of living in a world that feels both too dangerous and already over. What frightens him most is the thought that this might be permanent, that the version of himself who could laugh at a joke or look forward to a weekend is gone for good. He hopes, though he cannot quite say it out loud, that somewhere inside him there is still a person who believes in tomorrow.
